2.1.task: Sort these questions: A. How many minutes did one runner take on each of six practice days? B. What is the runner's recorded time on Monday? Identify the variable and explain which question anticipates variability.
2.1.key: A is statistical: the variable is daily running time in minutes, measured over six days, and times may vary. B requests one recorded value. A statistical investigation need not involve many different people.
2.1.stretch: Write a statistical question about classroom objects, and name the population and unit.
2.1.stretch_key: Example: What are the lengths, in centimeters, of the pencils in this box? Population: pencils in the box; variable: length; unit: centimeters; lengths may vary.
2.1.check: A gardener measures the height of every plant in one tray. Is 'How tall are the plants in this tray?' statistical? Explain.
2.1.check_key: Yes. The population is plants in the tray, the variable is height, and different heights are anticipated. State an appropriate unit such as centimeters.
2.1.error: Counts the number of people rather than deciding whether the measured values can vary.
2.1.feedback: Name what is measured, on which objects or occasions, and why its values could differ.
2.1.frame: The question is statistical because the values of ___ may ___.

2.1.task: Six observations are 2, 3, 3, 3, 5, 6 books. Complete the dot plot. Identify the peak and a gap. Explain how you know all observations are represented.
2.1.key: One dot at 2, three at 3, one at 5, one at 6; six dots total. Peak: 3 books. Gap within the observed range: 4 books. Each observation contributes exactly one dot.
2.1.stretch: Can adding one observation create a second value tied for the greatest frequency? Explain.
2.1.stretch_key: A single added observation cannot tie another value with the frequency 3 at the existing peak: frequencies at 2, 5, or 6 rise only to 2. Students should explain this impossibility rather than invent a second peak.
2.1.check: Data are 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 5. Describe the dots at 2 and 4 and state the total number of dots.
2.1.check_key: Two dots at 2; three at 4; seven dots total.
2.1.error: Plots one dot for each distinct value and loses repetitions.
2.1.feedback: Cross off one observation only after drawing its dot. Compare the observation count with the dot count.
2.1.frame: The peak is ___ because ___. The plot represents all ___ observations because ___.

2.2.task: Reading times are 0, 9, 10, 19, 20, 24, 29, 30 minutes. Use intervals 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, 30–39. Make a frequency table and histogram. Explain where 10 and 20 belong.
2.2.key: Frequencies are 2, 2, 3, 1. Ten belongs only in 10–19 and twenty only in 20–29. Eight observations are counted exactly once.
2.2.stretch: For measurements that include decimals, rewrite the intervals so 9.5 also has exactly one home.
2.2.stretch_key: Use 0 ≤ t < 10, 10 ≤ t < 20, 20 ≤ t < 30, and 30 ≤ t < 40. Then 9.5 belongs in the first interval.
2.2.check: Group 4, 10, 12, 20, 21, 28 into 0–9, 10–19, and 20–29. Give the frequencies and their sum.
2.2.error: Counts a boundary value in two intervals or leaves it out.
2.2.feedback: Underline each interval's endpoints. Assign each observation to one interval, then check the total.
2.2.frame: The value ___ belongs in ___ because its lower bound is ___ and its upper bound is ___.

2.2.task: The histogram has interval frequencies 1, 2, 4, 7 from left to right. Which side has the tail? Explain why the location of the tallest bar does not name the tail.
2.2.key: The tail extends left, toward the lower-frequency intervals. The highest bar is at the right, but skew is named for the tail, so this display is left-skewed.
2.2.stretch: Design four interval frequencies that make a symmetric histogram with eight observations.
2.2.stretch_key: One example is 1, 3, 3, 1. Mirrored frequencies give symmetry and total 8.
2.2.check: A histogram has frequencies 6, 4, 2, 1 from left to right. Name the tail and justify the shape.
2.2.check_key: Tail to the right; frequencies diminish toward larger values, so the display is right-skewed.
2.2.error: Names the skew for the side with the tallest bar.
2.2.feedback: Start at the cluster of high bars and trace the thinning bars outward; name that tail.
2.2.frame: The tail extends to the ___, so I describe the distribution as ___.

2.3.task: Order 9, 3, 7, 3, 8. Mark the middle position. Explain why the repeated 3 must be kept when finding the median.
2.3.key: Ordered data: 3, 3, 7, 8, 9. Median: 7. Both 3s are separate observations; removing one changes the data and the middle positions.
2.3.stretch: Change the greatest value to 90. Does the median change? Explain using positions.
2.3.stretch_key: No; the ordered values become 3, 3, 7, 8, 90. The third value remains 7.
2.3.check: Find the median of 12, 4, 9, 4, 6 and show the ordering.
2.3.error: Selects the middle entry before sorting or removes repeated observations.
2.3.feedback: Use one card for every observation, sort all cards, and mark the middle position.
2.3.frame: After ordering all ___ observations, the middle value is ___ because ___.

2.3.task: Order 8, 3, 12, 5. Locate the two middle values on a number line and mark their midpoint. Must the median be one of the observed values?
2.3.key: Ordered data: 3, 5, 8, 12. Median = (5 + 8) ÷ 2 = 6.5. The median need not be an observed value.
2.3.stretch: Create four whole-number observations with median 6.5 and verify your set.
2.3.stretch_key: Example: 2, 6, 7, 10; the middle pair averages to 6.5. Other valid sets are accepted.
2.3.check: Find the median of 4, 15, 10, 7 and explain which numbers you average.
2.3.error: Averages the minimum and maximum or selects only one middle value.
2.3.feedback: Number the sorted positions. For four observations, mark positions 2 and 3 before calculating.
2.3.frame: The median is between ___ and ___, so I calculate ___.

2.4.task: For 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, find the five-number summary and draw a box plot. When there is an odd number of observations, exclude the overall median from both halves.
2.4.key: Minimum 2, Q1 4, median 8, Q3 12, maximum 14. The box extends 4 to 12, with a median line at 8 and whiskers to 2 and 14.
2.4.stretch: Explain why the box does not reveal the exact individual observations inside it.
2.4.stretch_key: A box plot records five summaries, not every observation. Different data sets can share those summaries.
2.4.check: Find the five-number summary for 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15 using the stated convention.
2.4.error: Includes the overall median in the lower and upper halves despite the stated convention.
2.4.feedback: Circle the overall median and set it aside while finding the medians of the two remaining halves.
2.4.frame: I used ___ as the overall median; the lower half is ___, so Q1 is ___.

2.4.task: Compare the two box plots on the same scale. Which has the lower median? Which has the smaller middle-half spread? Can you tell which group has more observations?
2.4.key: A has median 8 and IQR 4; B has median 10 and IQR 8. A has the lower median and smaller middle-half spread. Sample sizes cannot be determined from these box plots alone.
2.4.stretch: Explain why equal-length boxes would not prove that two data sets are identical.
2.4.stretch_key: Equal box lengths show equal IQR only; medians, extremes, individual observations, and counts could differ.
2.4.check: A has Q1 5, median 7, Q3 9; B has Q1 4, median 8, Q3 12. Compare medians and IQRs.
2.4.check_key: A: median 7, IQR 4; B: median 8, IQR 8. A has a lower center and a less spread-out middle half.
2.4.error: Uses box length to infer the number of observations.
2.4.feedback: Label the axis as values, not counts. Ask which information a five-number summary does and does not contain.
2.4.frame: Group ___ has a smaller IQR because ___ − ___ = ___, compared with ___.

2.5.task: Use the medians of the lower and upper halves. Compare A: 1, 2, 3, 4 and B: 1, 2, 3, 40. Find each range and IQR. Is changing a maximum guaranteed to leave IQR unchanged?
2.5.key: A: range 3, Q1 1.5, Q3 3.5, IQR 2. B: range 39, Q1 1.5, Q3 21.5, IQR 20. No; in these small sets the maximum participates in Q3. The seven-value examples have different quartile positions.
2.5.stretch: Explain why replacing 7 by 70 in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 leaves IQR unchanged under this convention.
2.5.stretch_key: Q1 is 2 and Q3 is 6 in both seven-value sets. Their IQR is 4, although range increases from 6 to 69.
2.5.check: Compare IQRs for 2, 4, 6, 8 and 2, 4, 6, 20. Explain the effect of changing the maximum.
2.5.check_key: First: Q1 3, Q3 7, IQR 4. Second: Q1 3, Q3 13, IQR 10. It changes because the maximum is part of the upper-half median.
2.5.error: Treats resistance to extremes as a rule that IQR never changes.
2.5.feedback: Recompute the two quartiles and identify which observations determine them before making a claim.
2.5.frame: The IQR changed from ___ to ___ because Q3 ___. This shows that ___.

2.5.task: Two delivery routes have five-number summaries A: 2, 8, 10, 12, 40 and B: 5, 7, 11, 17, 25 minutes. Compare overall spread and middle-half spread. Which route is more consistent depends on which measure?
2.5.key: A: range 38 and IQR 4. B: range 20 and IQR 10. B has the smaller overall spread; A has the smaller middle-half spread. A claim must name the measure and purpose.
2.5.stretch: Recommend a route for someone who prioritizes a predictable typical trip, then explain what risk your choice does not capture.
2.5.stretch_key: A has the narrower middle half and lower median, but its maximum is much larger. B could be preferred by someone concerned with the largest observed wait.
2.5.check: X has range 30 and IQR 4; Y has range 18 and IQR 8. Which is less spread out overall, and which has the steadier middle half?
2.5.check_key: Y overall by range; X in the middle half by IQR.
2.5.error: Compares one group's range with another group's IQR or calls a group simply 'more spread out' without a measure.
2.5.feedback: Make two comparison rows: range versus range, and IQR versus IQR. Attach the purpose to each row.
2.5.frame: Using ___, I choose ___ because ___. However, the other measure shows ___.

2.6.task: Data A are 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. In data B, replace 8 with 28. Find each mean and median. Which is more resistant to this change, and what does 'typical' mean in your explanation?
2.6.key: A: mean 6, median 6. B: mean 10, median 6. The median did not change; the mean increased by 4. For a central individual value, the median is more representative here, while the mean still summarizes total divided by count.
2.6.stretch: When would the mean of B still be useful?
2.6.stretch_key: For fair sharing or total workload: five groups each taking the mean amount 10 would account for the total 50.
2.6.check: Compare mean and median of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 with 2, 3, 4, 5, 26.
2.6.check_key: First mean/median 4/4; second mean/median 8/4. Explain the different sensitivity to the extreme change.
2.6.error: Uses 'outlier means median' without considering the purpose or computing the summaries.
2.6.feedback: Ask whether the question is about a central observation, a fair share, or a total; use the matching evidence.
2.6.frame: For the purpose of ___, I use ___ because the change in the extreme value ___.

2.6.task: Queue A has median 7 minutes and IQR 8 minutes. Queue B has median 10 minutes and IQR 2 minutes. Recommend a queue for a person who values a shorter typical wait, then for a person who values consistent waits.
2.6.key: A has the shorter typical wait by median, 3 minutes less. B has the narrower middle-half spread, by 6 minutes. Either choice can be justified by the stated priority; neither summary guarantees an individual wait.
2.6.stretch: What additional information would help someone who must never wait longer than 15 minutes?
2.6.stretch_key: Maximum or upper-tail information and the actual context would help; medians and IQRs alone cannot guarantee a maximum wait.
2.6.check: A service has median 12 and IQR 3 minutes; another has median 9 and IQR 10. Explain one reason to choose each.
2.6.check_key: First for consistency of the middle half; second for the lower typical time. State that both measures summarize distributions, not guarantees.
2.6.error: Chooses the lower median without considering variability or claims a guaranteed wait.
2.6.feedback: Write one sentence about center and one about spread, then connect the recommendation to a stated priority.
2.6.frame: If the priority is ___, I recommend ___ because ___. The tradeoff is ___.

2.7.task: Share 7.2 meters of ribbon equally among 3 groups. Represent 7.2 as 72 tenths, divide, then connect that model to 7.2 ÷ 3. Estimate the answer and check by multiplication.
2.7.key: 72 tenths ÷ 3 = 24 tenths = 2.4 meters. An estimate is 6 ÷ 3 = 2, so 2.4 is reasonable. Check 2.4 × 3 = 7.2.
2.7.stretch: Explain why an answer of 24 meters is unreasonable before calculating exactly.
2.7.stretch_key: Each share must be less than the original 7.2 meters when dividing it into three positive equal shares; 24 exceeds the total.
2.7.check: Share 9.6 liters equally among 4 containers. Show a place-value explanation and multiplication check.
2.7.error: Divides whole-number digits correctly but loses the value represented by each digit.
2.7.feedback: Rename the amount in tenths and keep that unit through the division before renaming in whole units.
2.7.frame: I divided ___ tenths into ___ groups, so each group has ___ tenths, or ___.

2.7.task: How many 0.6-liter bottles can be filled from 4.8 liters? Rename both measures in tenths of a liter. Explain why scaling only the divisor would change the question.
2.7.key: 4.8 L is 48 tenths and 0.6 L is 6 tenths, so 48 ÷ 6 = 8 bottles. Scaling both numbers by 10 preserves their ratio; scaling only one changes it. Check 8 × 0.6 = 4.8.
2.7.stretch: Why is the quotient 8 larger than the numerical value 4.8?
2.7.stretch_key: The quotient counts bottles smaller than one liter. Dividing by a positive amount less than 1 can produce a larger numerical quotient.
2.7.check: How many 0.4-meter pieces fit in 3.2 meters? Explain an equivalent whole-number division.
2.7.error: Moves a decimal in only one number or assumes division always makes a number smaller.
2.7.feedback: Label both measurements in the same smaller unit and interpret what the quotient counts.
2.7.frame: Both quantities became ___ times as large numerically, but their ratio stayed ___ because ___.

2.8.task: Four groups collected 0, 2, 4, and 10 cans. Use a fair-share model to find the mean. Explain why the group with zero cans is still included in the divisor.
2.8.key: Total 16 cans, four groups; mean 4 cans per group. The zero contributes nothing to the total but is still one group sharing the total. A fair-share model redistributes 6 from the group with 10: 4 to the zero group and 2 to the group with 2.
2.8.stretch: Must a group actually have the mean number? Construct a two-group counterexample.
2.8.stretch_key: No. Groups with 1 and 2 cans have mean 1.5, which neither group has.
2.8.check: Find and interpret the mean of 0, 3, 6, 7 cans.
2.8.check_key: Total 16 divided by 4 = 4 cans per group; keep the zero observation in the count.
2.8.error: Leaves a zero observation out of the count.
2.8.feedback: Place one container for each group. Count the containers before redistributing the total.
2.8.frame: The mean is ___ per group because ___ objects are shared among ___ groups.

2.8.task: Three quiz scores are 6, 8, and 9. What fourth score gives a mean of 8? Each quiz has a maximum of 10. Could a fourth score produce a mean of 9? Explain.
2.8.key: For mean 8, target total is 4 × 8 = 32; current total 23; missing score 9. For mean 9, target total 36; missing score 13, impossible with a maximum of 10.
2.8.stretch: Find the greatest possible final mean and explain why it is a maximum.
2.8.stretch_key: (23 + 10) ÷ 4 = 8.25. No larger fourth score is allowed.
2.8.check: Scores are 5, 7, and 8. What fourth score gives a mean of 7? Check it.
2.8.error: Uses the number of known values rather than the final number of observations.
2.8.feedback: Draw four score slots, including the missing score. Multiply the desired mean by four before subtracting the known total.
2.8.frame: There will be ___ scores, so the target total is ___. The missing score is ___, which is/is not possible because ___.

2.9.task: Plant growth measurements are 2, 4, 6, and 8 centimeters. Find the mean, each distance from the mean, and the MAD. Explain why the distances do not cancel.
2.9.key: Mean 5 cm; distances 3, 1, 1, 3 cm; total distance 8 cm; MAD 2 cm. Distances are nonnegative; using signed differences would cancel and would not measure typical distance.
2.9.stretch: Explain the difference between the mean of 5 cm and MAD of 2 cm in one connected sentence.
2.9.stretch_key: The mean locates the center at 5 cm, while the MAD says observations are an average distance of 2 cm from that center.
2.9.check: Find the MAD of 3, 5, 7, 9 cm and interpret it.
2.9.check_key: Mean 6; distances 3,1,1,3; MAD 2 cm, the average distance from the mean.
2.9.error: Averages signed deviations or stops after adding the distances.
2.9.feedback: Draw each distance as a segment from the mean. Add lengths, then divide by the number of observations.
2.9.frame: The MAD is ___ because the total distance ___ is divided by ___. It describes ___.

2.9.task: A: 4, 5, 5, 6 and B: 1, 3, 7, 9 have the same mean. Compute their MADs and explain which set is more consistent around its mean.
2.9.key: Both means are 5. A distances 1,0,0,1: MAD 0.5. B distances 4,2,2,4: MAD 3. A is more tightly clustered around its mean.
2.9.stretch: Create four observations with mean 5 and MAD 0. Explain your set.
2.9.check: C: 6,8,8,10 and D: 2,6,10,14 both have mean 8. Compare their MADs.
2.9.check_key: C distances 2,0,0,2: MAD 1. D distances 6,2,2,6: MAD 4. C is more consistent around its mean.
2.9.error: Assumes equal means imply equal distributions or equal variability.
2.9.feedback: Keep the mean fixed, then compare every distance from it rather than recomputing only the centers.
2.9.frame: Both sets have mean ___, but set ___ has a smaller MAD, so ___.

2.10.task: Five families collected 2, 3, 4, 5, and 26 books. Find the mean and median. Choose a measure for a typical family's collection, then for dividing the total equally among five delivery boxes.
2.10.key: Total 40, mean 8, median 4. Median 4 is a useful central-family description because the large collection raises the mean. Mean 8 gives the equal share for five boxes. The purpose matters.
2.10.stretch: Explain why calling the mean 'wrong' because of an extreme value is misleading.
2.10.stretch_key: The mean is correctly calculated and answers total divided by count; it may be less useful for a particular description of a typical observation.
2.10.check: For 1,2,3,4,20, find mean and median and choose a center to describe a central individual value.
2.10.check_key: Mean 6, median 3; median is a defensible choice for a central individual value because the high value raises the mean.
2.10.error: Selects a measure mechanically without connecting it to the question.
2.10.feedback: Ask whether the decision needs a central observation or an equal share of the total, then compare both summaries.
2.10.frame: For ___ I choose the ___, because ___. For a different purpose, ___ could be useful.

2.10.task: Compare A: 4,6,8,10,12 and B: 4,6,8,10,32. Describe shape, choose a center/spread pair, and justify your choice for describing typical observations. Use the stated median-of-halves convention.
2.10.key: A is symmetric about 8: mean 8 and MAD 2.4 are useful. B has a large high value: median 8 and IQR 16 are defensible; Q1 5, Q3 21. Do not claim the IQR is unaffected merely because it is resistant.
2.10.stretch: How does the small sample affect a blanket claim that IQR ignores the largest value?
2.10.stretch_key: The upper half of B is 10,32, so Q3 depends on 32. Resistance is not immunity; compute and interpret the actual summaries.
2.10.check: For symmetric data 2,4,6,8,10, give mean and MAD and explain the pair.
2.10.check_key: Mean 6; distances 4,2,0,2,4; MAD 2.4. The pair describes center and average distance for the symmetric distribution.
2.10.error: Pairs a center and spread without inspecting shape or assumes a resistant measure never changes.
2.10.feedback: Sketch the data, compute the candidate summaries, and make the choice match the purpose and actual values.
2.10.frame: The distribution is ___, so I describe its center with ___ and its spread with ___ because ___.

3.1.task: A tray holds 4 blue counters and 6 yellow counters. Write blue:yellow, yellow:blue, and blue:all in simplest form. Explain what each number counts.
3.1.key: Blue:yellow = 4:6 = 2:3; yellow:blue = 6:4 = 3:2; blue:all = 4:10 = 2:5. Order and the meaning of the second quantity matter.
3.1.check: There are 3 red and 9 green counters. Give red:green and red:all in simplest form.
3.1.error: Uses the other part as the whole or reverses the requested order.
3.1.feedback: Label each color and circle the whole collection; say both quantity names before writing the ratio.
3.1.frame: The second term counts ___, so my ratio is ___ rather than ___.
3.1.stretch: Add equal numbers of blue and yellow counters. Must the ratio stay the same? Give a counterexample.
3.1.stretch_key: No. Adding 2 of each produces 6:8 = 3:4, different from 2:3. Equivalent ratios require the same multiplicative scale, not equal additions.

3.1.task: Split 35 stickers between two groups in the ratio 2:3. Label the equal tape units, find both shares, and check their sum.
3.1.key: Five equal units; 35 ÷ 5 = 7 per unit. Shares 14 and 21; 14 + 21 = 35 and 14:21 = 2:3.
3.1.check: Split 48 tickets in the ratio 1:3. Explain the value of one part.
3.1.check_key: Four parts; each 12 tickets; shares 12 and 36.
3.1.error: Divides the total by only one ratio term.
3.1.feedback: Count all equal tape units before finding the value of one unit.
3.1.frame: There are ___ equal parts in all, so one part is ___ and the shares are ___.
3.1.stretch: Create a different total that can be shared in ratio 2:3 using whole stickers.
3.1.stretch_key: Any positive multiple of 5 works, such as 40 with shares 16 and 24; explain the shared unit value.

3.2.task: A printer makes 84 pages in 6 minutes at a steady rate. Find pages per minute and minutes per page. Which rate directly answers how many pages it makes in 5 minutes?
3.2.key: 14 pages/minute and 1/14 minute/page. Use 14 pages/minute: 5 × 14 = 70 pages. Reciprocal rates have different meanings and units.
3.2.check: A machine makes 72 labels in 8 minutes. Find labels per minute and the number in 3 minutes.
3.2.error: Divides in the opposite order without changing the meaning of the unit.
3.2.feedback: Write the requested compound unit first; put the quantity named first in the numerator.
3.2.frame: I need ___ per ___, so I divide ___ by ___.
3.2.stretch: When would minutes per page be useful?
3.2.stretch_key: To find the time needed for a given number of pages; for example, 28 pages × 1/14 minute/page = 2 minutes.

3.2.task: Pack A contains 6 notebooks for $9.30. Pack B contains 8 for $12. Compare cost per notebook without rounding until the comparison is made. Which has the lower unit price?
3.2.key: A: $1.55/notebook; B: $1.50/notebook. B is lower by $0.05 per notebook.
3.2.check: Compare 4 pens for $3.20 with 6 pens for $4.50. Give both unit prices.
3.2.check_key: $0.80 and $0.75 per pen; the six-pack has the lower unit price.
3.2.error: Chooses the lower package price without matching quantities.
3.2.feedback: Reduce each package to the cost of one item, retaining dollars per item.
3.2.frame: Pack ___ is cheaper per notebook because ___ is less than ___.
3.2.stretch: If you need exactly 6 notebooks and can buy only whole packs, does the lower unit price guarantee a lower checkout cost?
3.2.stretch_key: No. One A pack costs $9.30 and supplies 6; one B costs $12 and supplies 8. The buying constraint changes the decision.

3.3.task: A recipe uses 3 cups of oats for 2 cups of seeds. Complete the table for 6, 9, and 12 cups of oats. Explain why adding 3 to both entries of 3:2 does not preserve the recipe.
3.3.key: Seeds: 4, 6, 8. Multiply both terms by 2, 3, or 4. Adding 3 gives 6:5, while the equivalent ratio for 6 cups oats is 6:4.
3.3.check: A ratio is 4:7. Complete the second quantity when the first is 8 and 12, and explain.
3.3.check_key: 14 and 21; both quantities scale by 2 and by 3.
3.3.error: Uses equal addition rather than equal scaling.
3.3.feedback: Draw matching scale-factor arrows on both quantities and check the original ratio.
3.3.frame: Both quantities are multiplied by ___, so the relationship remains ___.
3.3.stretch: Find an equivalent pair with less than 3 cups of oats.
3.3.stretch_key: Example: 1.5 cups oats and 1 cup seeds; divide both terms by 2.

3.3.task: A mixture uses 6 cups of nuts for 8 cups of raisins. Find the raisins for 15 cups of nuts using a bridge through 3 cups and using a scale factor. Compare the methods.
3.3.key: Bridge: 6:8 ÷ 2 = 3:4, then × 5 = 15:20. Direct factor 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5; 8 × 2.5 = 20. Both preserve the ratio.
3.3.check: A mixture is 8:12. Find the second quantity when the first is 14; show a bridge or unit rate.
3.3.check_key: 21; for example divide by 4 to get 2:3, then multiply by 7.
3.3.error: Assumes the scale factor must be a whole number.
3.3.feedback: Choose an equivalent pair whose first term divides the target, or compute the unit rate.
3.3.frame: I used the bridge ___ because it connects ___ to ___ with ___.
3.3.stretch: Which method is more efficient for 1.5 cups of nuts? Justify a valid method.
3.3.stretch_key: Divide 6:8 by 4 to get 1.5:2; 2 cups raisins. Efficiency judgments may differ if the arithmetic is valid.

3.4.task: Each full tray holds 6 muffins. Complete a table for 0, 1, 2, and 3 full trays, then plot its points. Label both axes and explain the origin.
3.4.key: Points (0,0),(1,6),(2,12),(3,18). Horizontal: full trays; vertical: muffins. With zero trays there are zero muffins in this model.
3.4.check: Each bag contains 5 beads. Give the points for 0, 2, and 4 bags and interpret (2,10).
3.4.error: Swaps the coordinates or omits contextual units.
3.4.feedback: Read each table row as (number of trays, number of muffins), then move horizontally before vertically.
3.4.frame: The point (___, ___) means ___ trays hold ___ muffins.
3.4.stretch: Is (1.5,9) a possible order if only full trays are sold?
3.4.stretch_key: It fits the numerical ratio but is not a permitted order of full trays. Plot discrete whole-tray possibilities for this context.

3.4.task: Apples cost $3 per pound. Plot (1,3),(2,6),(4,12). Explain (4,12), decide whether (3,10) belongs to the relationship, and find the cost of 2.5 pounds.
3.4.key: Four pounds cost $12. (3,10) is not on this relationship because 3 pounds cost $9. Cost of 2.5 pounds is $7.50; fractional pounds are meaningful here.
3.4.check: A rate is $4 per kilogram. Does (3,12) fit? Does (3,15)? Explain both with units.
3.4.check_key: (3,12) fits: 3 kg cost $12. (3,15) does not; at the stated rate the cost is $12.
3.4.error: Accepts a point because it is near the line without checking the ratio.
3.4.feedback: Divide cost by mass or multiply the known rate by the point's input and compare the output.
3.4.frame: The point ___ fits/does not fit because ___ dollars per pound gives ___.
3.4.stretch: Compare why intermediate points are meaningful for apples but not full trays of muffins.
3.4.stretch_key: Apples may be weighed in fractional pounds; a whole-tray sales rule restricts tray counts to whole numbers.

3.5.task: Mix A uses 2 cups of concentrate for 5 cups of water. Mix B uses 3 cups for 7 cups of water. Compare them using 6 cups of concentrate in each. Which tastes stronger if strength means more concentrate per cup of water?
3.5.key: A becomes 6:15; B becomes 6:14. B is stronger because it uses less water for the same concentrate. Keep concentrate:water distinct from concentrate:total mixture.
3.5.check: A uses 1 cup concentrate to 3 cups water; B uses 2 to 5. Compare with 2 cups concentrate.
3.5.check_key: A 2:6, B 2:5; B is stronger under the stated definition.
3.5.error: Compares unequal reference amounts or confuses the water with the total mixture.
3.5.feedback: Label the common quantity in both rows, then compare only the corresponding other quantities.
3.5.frame: For the same ___ cups of concentrate, ___ uses ___ water, so ___.
3.5.stretch: Could you compare using a common water amount instead? Show one valid comparison.
3.5.stretch_key: Use 35 cups water: A 14 cups concentrate, B 15. B remains stronger.

3.5.task: Hose A fills 8 gallons in 2 minutes; B fills 15 gallons in 5 minutes. Compare at 10 minutes and by unit rate. Explain why both methods agree.
3.5.key: At 10 minutes A fills 40 gallons and B 30. Unit rates are 4 and 3 gallons/minute. A is faster; both methods compare equal times.
3.5.check: A makes 18 items in 3 minutes; B makes 28 in 4. Which is faster? Show a common-time or unit-rate comparison.
3.5.check_key: A 6 items/minute; B 7. B is faster. At 12 minutes: 72 versus 84 items.
3.5.error: Selects the larger produced quantity without considering elapsed time.
3.5.feedback: Put both outputs over one common time before comparing.
3.5.frame: I compared ___ minutes for both, which gives ___ and ___, so ___.
3.5.stretch: Give a different common-time benchmark and explain why it produces the same decision.
3.5.stretch_key: At 20 minutes A fills 80 gallons and B 60; equal scaling preserves the comparison.

3.6.task: A banner needs 8 feet of ribbon. Ribbon is sold only by the whole yard. Use 1 yard = 3 feet to find the exact length in yards and the purchase amount. Check whether 2 yards would be enough.
3.6.key: 8 ÷ 3 = 2 2/3 yards; buy 3 whole yards. Two yards is 6 feet, which is insufficient. The purchase is 9 feet, leaving 1 foot.
3.6.check: A project needs 14 feet. How many whole yards should be bought? Explain and check the smaller whole-number choice.
3.6.check_key: Buy 5 yards = 15 feet; 4 yards = 12 feet is not enough.
3.6.error: Rounds a required purchase down or uses the wrong unit fact.
3.6.feedback: Write the equality 1 yd = 3 ft; test the neighboring whole-yard purchase amounts against the needed feet.
3.6.frame: The exact length is ___ yards, but I buy ___ because ___ would not be enough.
3.6.stretch: Explain why ounces of mass and fluid ounces of volume cannot be interchanged just because both use 'ounce'.
3.6.stretch_key: They measure different quantities: mass/weight versus volume. A conversion must connect units of the same measured quantity or provide a context-specific relationship.

3.6.task: A container holds 1.5 liters. Cups hold 250 milliliters each. Complete the equivalent-measure table, find the number of cups, and explain why changing units does not change the amount of liquid.
3.6.key: 1 L = 1000 mL; 0.5 L = 500 mL; 1.5 L = 1500 mL. 1500 ÷ 250 = 6 cups. Smaller units produce a larger numerical measure of the same quantity.
3.6.check: A bottle holds 0.8 L. How many 200 mL cups can it fill? Explain the unit conversion first.
3.6.error: Divides numbers expressed in different units or moves a decimal without identifying a scale factor.
3.6.feedback: Rename both quantities in milliliters, then interpret how many equal portions fit.
3.6.frame: The numerical measure changed from ___ to ___, but the quantity stayed the same because ___.
3.6.stretch_key: 1 × 1000 + 0.5 × 1000 = 1000 + 500 = 1500; each part is scaled by the same factor.

3.7.task: Use 1 kilogram ≈ 2.2 pounds. A package weighs 15.4 pounds. Find its approximate mass in kilograms. Explain the operation, approximation symbol, and a reverse check.
3.7.key: 15.4 ÷ 2.2 = 7, so 15.4 lb ≈ 7 kg. A kilogram corresponds to more than one pound, so the numerical measure decreases. Check 7 × 2.2 = 15.4 using the approximate factor.
3.7.check: Using the same factor, convert 19.8 pounds to kilograms and check.
3.7.check_key: Approximately 9 kg; 9 × 2.2 = 19.8 lb using the supplied approximation.
3.7.error: Uses an exact-equality claim for an approximate cross-system factor or multiplies in the wrong direction.
3.7.feedback: Build the given equivalent pair and scale it to the target while keeping ≈ visible.
3.7.frame: The mass is approximately ___ because ___; I use ≈ since ___.
3.7.stretch: Why does exact division of the supplied numbers not make the real-world conversion exact?
3.7.stretch_key: The factor 2.2 is itself approximate. Exact arithmetic with a rounded factor still produces an approximate conversion.

3.7.task: A craft mixture uses 3 grams of pigment per kilogram of clay. You have 11 pounds of clay. Use 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb. Pigment is supplied at 5 grams per scoop. About how many scoops are needed? Show a path through the units.
3.7.key: 11 lb ≈ 5 kg; 5 × 3 = 15 g pigment; 15 ÷ 5 = 3 scoops. The unit path is pounds → kilograms → grams pigment → scoops. The result is approximate because the conversion factor is approximate.
3.7.check: There are 17.6 lb of clay, 2 g pigment per kg, and 4 g per scoop. Using 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb, find scoops.
3.7.error: Uses the rate before converting its reference quantity or confuses grams of pigment with grams of clay.
3.7.feedback: Label the substance as well as the unit at each step, and match each rate's input to the previous output.
3.7.frame: I first convert ___ to ___ so that the rate ___ can be applied. Then ___.
3.7.stretch: Explain why rounding a conversion too early can change the final amount in another problem.
3.7.stretch_key: An early rounded intermediate value changes the input to later operations; keep the available precision until the requested final rounding.

4.1.task: A team finished 9 of 12 challenges at field day. Use the bar to show what percent of the challenges they finished. a. Write the missing numbers under the bar. Shade 9 challenges. b. What percent of the challenges did the team finish? c. Explain how you know.
4.1.key: a. 3, 6, 9; shade 3 of the 4 parts.  b. 75%  c. All 12 challenges are the whole, 100%. Each part is 3 challenges, or 25%. 9 challenges fill 3 parts, so 3 × 25% = 75%.
4.1.check: A soccer team won 12 of its 15 games. What percent of its games did it win? Name the whole.
4.1.check_key: The whole is 15 games (100%). 12 out of 15 = 4 out of 5 = 80 out of 100, so 80%.
4.1.error: Uses the part as the percent when the whole is not 100 (writes 9 of 12 as 9%).
4.1.feedback: Label the full bar 100% and the total count first, then split it into equal parts and name the percent of one part.
4.1.frame: Partner A: “The whole is ___ challenges, so each part is ___%.” Partner B: “9 challenges fill ___ parts, so the team finished ___%.”
4.1.stretch: Sam says 9 of 12 challenges is 9%. Use the bar to show why that is too small.
4.1.stretch_key: One part of the bar is already 25%, so 9% would be less than one part. 9 challenges fill 3 of the 4 parts, so the team finished 75%, not 9%.
exit_next: Write 7 out of 10 and 12 out of 50 as percents.
In a class, 9 out of 25 students bike to school. What percent bike? What percent do not bike?
Which percent is the same as 2 out of 5? Explain how you know.

frames.because: I know the whole is ___ because ___.
frames.but: Some students think 9 of 12 is 9%, but ___.
frames.so: Each part of the bar is ___%, so ___.

4.1.task: A gray kitten weighs 8 ounces. Its brother weighs 14 ounces. Use the bar to show the brother’s weight as a percent of the gray kitten’s weight. a. Fill in the percents. Shade the bar up to 14 ounces. b. The brother weighs what percent of the gray kitten’s weight? c. Explain how you know.
4.1.key: a. 25%, 50%, 75%, 125%, 150%, 175%; shade 7 of the 8 parts.  b. 175%  c. The gray kitten (8 ounces) is the whole, 100%. Each part is 2 ounces, or 25%. 14 ounces is 7 parts, so 7 × 25% = 175%. The brother is more than one whole, so the percent is more than 100%.
4.1.check: A food drive collected 60 cans in week 1 and 135 cans in week 2. Week 2 is what percent of week 1? Name the whole.
4.1.check_key: The whole is week 1, 60 cans (100%). 135 ÷ 60 = 2.25, so week 2 is 225% of week 1.
4.1.error: Thinks a percent can never be more than 100%, or writes the amount as the percent (writes 14 ounces as 14%).
4.1.feedback: Draw one bar for the whole labeled 100%, add a second whole bar ending at 200%, and have students shade the new amount across both bars.
4.1.frame: Partner A: “The whole is ___ ounces, so each part is ___%.” Partner B: “14 ounces fills ___ parts, so it is ___%, more than 100%.”
4.1.stretch: Ali says the brother weighs 14% of the gray kitten’s weight. Use the bar to show why that is too small.
4.1.stretch_key: 14% is less than one part of the bar (25%, or 2 ounces). The brother is heavier than the gray kitten, so his weight must be more than 100%. He fills 7 parts: 175%.
exit_next: Write 3.5 times as much and 1.75 times as much as percents.
A team scored 30 points in game 1 (the whole) and 48 points in game 2. Game 2 is what percent of game 1?
Which number is 300% of 12? Explain how you know.

frames.because: I know ___ is the whole because ___.
frames.but: Some students think a percent cannot be more than 100%, but ___.
frames.so: The brother weighs more than one whole, so ___.

4.2.task: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. Mia eats 3 slices. Fill in the percent row on the bar. Then write the part she ate as a fraction, a decimal, and a percent. a. What percent is 1 slice? What percent are 3 slices? b. Write 3/8 as a decimal. c. Explain how you know.
4.2.check: A school sold 33 of its 50 raffle tickets. Write the part sold as a fraction, a decimal, and a percent.
4.2.error: Writes the digits without thinking about the value: writes 3/8 as 0.38 or 38%, 0.08 as 80%, or 26 of 40 as 26%.
4.2.feedback: Have the student label an 8-part bar in 12.5% steps, point to 3 parts, and read the percent before writing any decimal.
4.2.frame: Partner A: “3/8 of the pizza is ___% because ___.” Partner B: “Show me on the bar where you see that.”
4.2.stretch: Sam says 3/8 = 38% because you put the 3 and the 8 together. Use the bar to show why Sam is wrong.
4.2.stretch_key: Each slice is 12.5%, so 3 slices are 3 × 12.5% = 37.5%, not 38%. Writing the digits 3 and 8 side by side does not keep the value: 38% = 38/100, but 3/8 = 37.5/100.
exit_next: Write 0.9 and 0.09 as percents. Explain why they are different.
Ming answered 22 of 25 questions correctly. Write her score as a percent. Did she do better than Kofi’s 72%?
Which two of these equal 40%: 0.04, 4/10, 2/5, 4/100? Explain.

frames.because: I know 3/8 = ___% because each slice is ___%.
frames.so: Each slice is 12.5%, so 3 slices are ___%.

4.2.task: Class A recycled 0.45 of its bottles. Class B recycled 2/5. Class C recycled 48%. Mark each value on the number line. Then order the classes from least to greatest. a. Write each value as a percent. b. Order the classes from least to greatest. c. Explain how you know.
4.2.key: a. 0.45 = 45%; 2/5 = 40/100 = 40%; 48% = 48%. b. Class B (2/5), Class A (0.45), Class C (48%). c. With all three as percents, 40% < 45% < 48%. On the line, 2/5 sits at 40%, 0.45 at 45%, and 48% is farthest right.
4.2.check: Three seed trays sprouted 0.27, 13/50, and 31% of their seeds. Order the values from least to greatest. Explain one comparison.
4.2.error: Compares the digits that show instead of the values (2/5 > 0.45 because 5 > 4; 0.4 < 39% because 4 < 39).
4.2.feedback: Have the student rewrite every value as a percent, mark each one on the same number line, and read the order from left to right.
4.2.frame: Partner A: “I wrote every value as a percent: ___, ___, ___. So the order is ___.” Partner B: “Which value is closest to 50%? How do you know?”
4.2.stretch: Leo says 2/5 is greater than 0.45 because 5 is greater than 4. Show why Leo is wrong.
4.2.stretch_key: Leo compared single digits, not values. 2/5 = 40/100 = 40% and 0.45 = 45%. 40% < 45%, so 2/5 is less than 0.45.
exit_next: Write <, >, or =: 0.5 ___ 49%. Explain using hundredths.
Add 0.37 to the list 0.35, 3/8, 36%. Where does it go in the order?
Which is the least: 0.7, 3/4, 72%, or 0.68? Explain how you know.

frames.because: I know ___ is greater than ___ because ___% > ___%.
frames.but: Some students think 2/5 is greater because 5 > 4, but ___.
frames.so: In percents the values are ___ < ___ < ___, so the order is ___.

4.3.task: A water tank holds 120 gallons. It has 82 gallons in it. About what percent of the tank is full? Use the bar to find benchmark amounts. a. Between which two benchmarks is 82 gallons? b. Use 10% of 120 to give a closer estimate. c. Explain how you know.
4.3.key: Bar: 30, 60, 90 gallons. a. Between 50% (60 gallons) and 75% (90 gallons); 82 is closer to 90, so about 75%. b. 10% of 120 = 12, so 70% = 7 × 12 = 84 gallons. 82 is close to 84, so about 70% (exact: about 68%). c. I found the benchmark amounts of 120 and compared 82 to them. 70% and 75% are both good estimates when the student names the benchmark amount used.
4.3.check: A garden has 56 tomato plants. 13 of them have ripe tomatoes. About what percent have ripe tomatoes? Name the benchmark amount you used.
4.3.check_key: 25% of 56 = 56 ÷ 4 = 14. 13 is close to 14, so about 25% (exact: about 23%).
4.3.error: Writes the part as the percent without using the whole (82 out of 120 called “82%”), or picks a benchmark without finding the benchmark amounts first.
4.3.feedback: Draw a bar for the whole, have the student label the 25%, 50%, and 75% amounts, and ask them to point to where the part falls before naming a percent.
4.3.frame: Partner A: “The whole is ___. The part is close to ___, which is ___% of the whole.” Partner B: “How do you know it is closer to ___% than to ___%?”
4.3.stretch: Sam says 82 out of 120 is about 82%. Show why that is too big.
4.3.stretch_key: 82% would mean 82 out of 100, but the whole here is 120, not 100. 82% of 120 is about 98 gallons, much more than 82. 82 is close to 84 = 70% of 120, so the tank is about 70% full.
exit_next: Between which two benchmarks is 31 out of 40? Which one is it closer to? Use 10% of 40 to check.
About what percent of the 300 beads are NOT used? Show the benchmark amount.
Is 19 out of 40 a little more or a little less than 50%? How do you know?

frames.because: I know ___ out of ___ is about ___% because ___% of ___ is ___.
frames.but: Some students think 82 out of 120 is 82%, but the whole is ___, so ___.
frames.so: ___ is between ___ and ___, so the percent is between ___% and ___%.

4.3.task: A theater sold 588 tickets. About 26% were for kids. Estimate the number of kids’ tickets two ways, using different compatible (friendly) numbers. a. Estimate with 25% of 600. b. Estimate with 25% of 560. c. Which estimate is closer? Explain how you know.
4.3.key: a. 600 ÷ 4 = about 150 tickets. b. 560 ÷ 4 = about 140 tickets. c. 150 is closer (exact: about 153), because 600 is closer to 588 than 560 is, and 26% is close to 25%. Both are reasonable estimates; give credit for the compatible numbers and the reasoning.
4.3.check: Estimate 49% of 818 in two ways. Name the compatible (friendly) numbers you used each time.
4.3.check_key: Examples: 50% of 800 = 400; 50% of 820 = 410. Exact: about 401. Accept any close estimate with named compatible numbers.
4.3.error: Believes there is just one right estimate and erases a reasonable one (says 140 is wrong for 26% of 588 because a classmate got 150), or moves the decimal the wrong way when finding 10%.
4.3.feedback: Put two estimates side by side, ask which rounded numbers each one used, and decide together which is closer to the exact answer and why.
4.3.frame: Partner A: “I used ___% of ___ because ___.” Partner B: “I used ___% of ___. Our estimates are different because ___.”
4.3.stretch: Sam says 150% of 58 is about 30, because 150% means take half. Show why that is too small.
4.3.stretch_key: 150% is more than the whole (100%), so the answer must be more than 58. Round to 60: 100% of 60 = 60 and 50% of 60 = 30, so 150% of 60 = 60 + 30 = 90. 150% of 58 is about 90. 30 is only 50%.
exit_next: Is your estimate for 76% of 41 high or low? Which rounding tells you?
Now estimate the sale price of the backpack. Is it a little high or a little low?
Estimate 20% of 390 a second way, using 10% first. Which estimate is closer?

frames.because: I rounded ___ to ___ because ___ is easy to divide by ___.
frames.but: Some students think only one estimate is right, but ___ and ___ are both close because ___.
frames.so: I rounded ___ up, so my estimate is a little ___.

4.4.task: A theater has 360 seats. 35% of the seats are in the balcony. Use the percent bar and an equation to find how many seats are in the balcony. a. Fill in the bar. What are 10% and 5% of 360? Use them to find 35%. b. Write and solve an equation: part = percent × whole. c. Explain how you know both ways give the same answer.
4.4.key: a. Bar: 36, 72, 108, 144, 180, 216, 252, 288, 324. 10% of 360 = 36 and 5% = 18, so 35% = 36 + 36 + 36 + 18 = 126 seats. b. part = 0.35 × 360 = 126 seats. c. Both ways take 35 out of every 100 parts of the same whole, 360: 0.35 = 0.10 + 0.10 + 0.10 + 0.05. 126 is less than half of 360 (180), so it makes sense.
4.4.check: A library got 220 new books. 15% are mysteries. How many are mysteries? Use 10% and 5%, then check with an equation.
4.4.error: Multiplies by the percent number instead of its decimal (35 × 360 = 12,600), or writes a one-digit percent as tenths (6% as 0.6), so the part is bigger than the whole or 10 times too big.
4.4.feedback: Have the student find 10% of the whole on a 10-part percent bar, build the percent from it, and check that the part is less than the whole before multiplying by the decimal.
4.4.frame: Partner A: “The whole is ___. 10% of it is ___, so 35% is ___.” Partner B: “Check with an equation: ___ × ___ = ___. Is the part less than the whole?”
4.4.stretch: Sam says 35% of 360 is 35 × 360 = 12,600. Show why that is too big.
4.4.stretch_key: 35% is less than half, so the part must be less than 180 (half of 360). 12,600 is more than all 360 seats. Sam multiplied by 35 instead of 0.35. 0.35 × 360 = 126 seats.
exit_next: You found 40% of 90 and 5% of 600. Find 10% of each whole first (9 and 60). How do 4 × 9 and half of 60 give the same answers?
Is the 6% tax on $45 closer to $2.70 or $27? Write 6% as a decimal (0.06, not 0.6) and explain.
Why is 15 × 60 = 900 far too big for 15% of 60? Write 15% as 0.15 and find the part.

frames.so: 35% is less than half of the whole, so ___.

4.4.task: Kira made 36 of 60 free throws. Dev made 32 of 40. Kira made more. Shade each bar to show each percent. Who is the better shooter? a. Write each record (how many out of how many) as a percent. b. Who has the better rate? c. Explain how you know.
4.4.key: a. Kira: 36/60 = 6/10 = 60/100 = 60% (shade 6 of 10 parts). Dev: 32/40 = 8/10 = 80/100 = 80% (shade 8 of 10 parts). b. Dev. c. Kira made more free throws, but she also took more shots (60 vs. 40). Each percent compares the part to its own whole, and 80% > 60%.
4.4.check: Zoe got 19 of 20 quiz questions right. Max got 46 of 50 right. Who did better? Show both percents.
4.4.check_key: Zoe: 19/20 = 95/100 = 95%. Max: 46/50 = 92/100 = 92%. Zoe did better, even though Max got more questions right.
4.4.error: Ranks records by the count made (36 > 32) and ignores the number of tries (60 vs. 40), or compares the part to 100 instead of to its own whole (33 of 55 called 33%).
4.4.feedback: Draw two equal 10-part bars, shade each player’s makes out of their own tries, and ask which bar is fuller.
4.4.frame: Partner A: “___ out of ___ is ___%, and ___ out of ___ is ___%.” Partner B: “So who did better? Why doesn’t the bigger count decide it?”
4.4.stretch: Lin says 54 out of 60 is better than 9 out of 10 because 54 is more than 9. Show why she is wrong.
4.4.stretch_key: 54/60 = 9/10 = 90/100 = 90%, and 9 out of 10 = 90%. The two records tie. 54 is bigger only because its whole (60) is bigger.
exit_next: 27 out of 30 and 7 out of 20: what do you multiply each bottom number by to get 100? Write each record as ___ out of 100.
Team B won more games (21) than Team A (15). Use 75% and 70% to explain why Team A still has the better record.
43 out of 50 has the biggest top number. Write 17/20, 22/25, 43/50 and 8/10 out of 100. Which is greatest, and why is it not 43 out of 50?

frames.because: I know ___ is the better shooter because ___% > ___%.
frames.but: Some students think ___ is better because ___, but ___.
frames.so: The two wholes are different, so ___.

4.5.task: A bike club has saved $27 for a trip. That is 30% of the money it needs. How much money does the club need in all? a. How much money is 10%? b. How much money does the club need in all? c. Explain how you know.
4.5.key: a. 30% is 3 parts of 10%, so 10% = $27 ÷ 3 = $9.  b. 100% is 10 parts: $9 × 10 = $90.  c. One part of the bar is $9, and the whole bar is 10 parts, so the whole is $90. Check: 0.30 × 90 = 27. The whole is greater than $27 because 30% is less than 100%.
4.5.check: A library has lent out 43 laptops. That is 20% of all its laptops. How many laptops does the library have?
4.5.error: Treats the known part as the whole or multiplies it by the percent (0.3 × 27 = $8.10), so the answer is smaller than the part.
4.5.feedback: Have the student write $27 under the shaded 30% section and ask whether the end of the bar (100%) must be more or less than $27 before any computing.
4.5.frame: Partner A: “The part is ___. It is ___% of the whole.” Partner B: “So 10% is ___, and 100% is ___.” Then switch.
4.5.stretch: Sam says the club needs 0.3 × 27 = $8.10. Show why that is too small.
4.5.stretch_key: $8.10 is less than the $27 the club already has, but the whole must be greater than the part. Sam multiplied when he should divide: 27 ÷ 0.3 = 90, so the club needs $90.
exit_next: 11 is 10% and 9 is 25%. Why do you multiply one by 10 and the other by 4?
Show 28 games as 40% on a 10-part bar. What does one part stand for?
Make up a part that is 50% of a whole. Is your whole more or less than the part? Explain.

frames.but: Some students think the whole is ___, but the whole must be greater than the part because ___.
frames.so: One part of the bar is ___, so all 10 parts are ___.

4.5.task: A runner has run 9 km. That is 45% of the whole race. Write an equation with *w* for the whole race. Solve it. a. Write an equation for the race. b. Solve for *w*. c. Explain how you know your answer makes sense.
4.5.key: a. 0.45 × w = 9  b. w = 9 ÷ 0.45 = 900 ÷ 45 = 20 km  c. Check: 0.45 × 20 = 9. The whole race (20 km) is greater than the 9 km part. 45% is a little less than half, so the race is a little more than 2 × 9 = 18 km.
4.5.check: A team has sold 87 T-shirts. That is 75% of its goal. Write and solve an equation for the goal.
4.5.error: Writes the percent as a whole number (45 × w = 9) or multiplies the part by the decimal (w = 0.45 × 9 = 4.05) instead of dividing the part by the decimal.
4.5.feedback: Point to the bar: the 9 km is the shaded 45% and w is the whole bar, so write 0.45 × w = 9 and ask what undoes multiplying by 0.45.
4.5.frame: Partner A: “The part is ___ and the percent is ___.” Partner B writes ___ × *w* = ___ and solves. Both check: ___ × ___ = ___.
4.5.stretch: Lin wrote 45 × *w* = 9. Show why her *w* is far too small. Then fix her equation.
4.5.stretch_key: 45 × w = 9 gives w = 0.2 km, which is less than the 9 km already run. 45% must be written as the decimal 0.45: 0.45 × w = 9, so w = 20 km.
exit_next: Solve 0.25 × w = 13 another way: 25% is one fourth, so what do you multiply 13 by?
Check the bike: what is 60% of your first price? Is it $138?
Someone chose 6.4 for 16 = 0.4w. What did they do, and how can you tell it is wrong?

frames.but: Some students multiply ___ by ___, but the whole must be greater than ___.

5.1.task: A parallelogram has base 8 cm, perpendicular height 3 cm, and slanted side 5 cm. Sketch a cut-and-slide rearrangement into a rectangle and find its area.
5.1.key: Area 8 × 3 = 24 cm². Rearranging a triangular piece preserves area and makes a rectangle with the same base and perpendicular height; the slanted side is not used.
5.1.check: A parallelogram has base 11 m, perpendicular height 4 m, side 6 m. Find area and explain the unused measure.
5.1.check_key: 44 m²; the 6 m side is not the perpendicular height.
5.1.error: Uses the slanted side as height.
5.1.feedback: Mark a right angle at the height and compare it with the rectangle produced by rearranging.
5.1.frame: The relevant faces or regions are ___ because ___. My labeled dimensions show ___, so the measure is ___.
5.1.stretch: Create a contrasting example that exposes the misconception: uses the slanted side as height.. Explain what changes and what stays true.
5.1.stretch_key: Accept a mathematically valid contrasting example and an explanation that uses the conditions in this session. Teacher anchor: Area 8 × 3 = 24 cm². Rearranging a triangular piece preserves area and makes a rectangle with the same base and perpendicular height; the slanted side is not used.

5.1.task: A rhombus has diagonals 12 cm and 8 cm. Split it into four right triangles and explain the diagonal formula.
5.1.key: Half-diagonals are 6 and 4; each triangle has area 12 cm²; four total 48 cm². This equals 12 × 8 ÷ 2.
5.1.check: Find a rhombus area with diagonals 10 m and 6 m; explain the factor one-half.
5.1.check_key: 30 m²; four half-diagonal right triangles give half the full diagonal product.
5.1.error: Treats diagonals as the base and perpendicular height of a rectangle.
5.1.feedback: Label the four half-diagonal triangles and count each region once.
5.1.frame: The relevant faces or regions are ___ because ___. My labeled dimensions show ___, so the measure is ___.
5.1.stretch: Create a contrasting example that exposes the misconception: treats diagonals as the base and perpendicular height of a rectangle.. Explain what changes and what stays true.
5.1.stretch_key: Accept a mathematically valid contrasting example and an explanation that uses the conditions in this session. Teacher anchor: Half-diagonals are 6 and 4; each triangle has area 12 cm²; four total 48 cm². This equals 12 × 8 ÷ 2.

5.2.task: Two congruent triangles with base 10 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm form a parallelogram. Find one triangle area and explain the factor one-half.
5.2.key: Parallelogram area 60 cm²; one triangle 30 cm². Each triangle is half of the parallelogram.
